purpose: Small source-traceable starter corpus, not a comprehensive account or independent archaeological peer review.
editorialNotes: Reviewed here means source passages and metadata checked at the access level recorded below; it does not mean that disputed claims are scientifically verified.
Astronomical year = 1950 - calibrated BP. BCE display = 1 - astronomical year for astronomical years <= 0. Do not convert uncalibrated radiocarbon ages this way.
Coordinates are public approximate locators, not excavation coordinates. White Sands deliberately uses the visitor-center locator and must say so on its review page.
Do not draw migration arrows from these records automatically. The starter corpus includes a historical event, fulfilling the requested movement-or-event example without inventing migration routes.
All review prose below is concise original paraphrase. Do not copy publication abstracts or PDFs into the distribution.
Important current development: Monte Verde II's late-Pleistocene chronology is actively disputed by a March 2026 Science paper and subsequent scholarly rebuttals. Do not label it uncontested.
Current White Sands sequence uses the October 2026 paper's 23.5–21.7 ka interval, not the earlier rounded 23–21 ka range.
Institutional coordinate and archive sources are used for location or primary-document provenance, not as substitutes for scientific dating publications.

sources.authors: Ciprian F. Ardelean, Lorena Becerra-Valdivia, Mikkel Winther Pedersen, et al.
sources.title: Evidence of human occupation in Mexico around the Last Glacial Maximum
sources.access: Publisher abstract/metadata and author-uploaded full-text version read. The upload identifies Ciprian F. Ardelean as uploader. Chronology section and reporting summary inspected.
sources.locator: Chronology section, Fig. 2, reporting summary Location
sources.supports: Reported lithic assemblage; modelled onset of SC-C at 33,150–31,405 cal BP, 95.4% probability; public WGS84 locator 24.61666, -101.13333.
sources.caveat: A modelled stratigraphic boundary is not a directly dated arrival or an uninterrupted occupation. Human manufacture is contested.

sources.access: University of Montana publication record, author list, publication metadata, and complete abstract read. Full article was not independently inspected.
sources.supports: The authors explicitly compare human manufacture with natural disintegration, roof fall, and mass movement, and favor the natural-process explanation.

sources.caveat: Earlier seed measurements and the independent checks belong to the same site chronology and are not independent evidence for a migration route.

records.title: Chiquihuite Cave — proposed onset of early human activity
records.coordinatePrecision: Approximate public locator, rounded to 0.01 degrees; not an excavation point

time.original: Modelled start of SC-C: 33,150–31,405 cal BP (95.4%)
time.method: Bayesian age model of radiocarbon determinations with OSL chronological control
time.conversion: 1950 minus calibrated BP; a possible onset interval, not a 1,746-year occupation

records.claim: The excavators interpret lithic material and its stratigraphic chronology as evidence of human activity beginning before the Last Glacial Maximum.
records.explanation: Ardelean and colleagues report a stone assemblage with a modelled early boundary in SC-C. This row shows that proposed boundary only. It does not assert continuous residence or a known ethnic identity.
records.discussion: The central dispute concerns whether the stones were made by people. Chatters and colleagues favor natural fragmentation and cave processes. A dated sediment sequence does not, by itself, resolve human agency. Treat this as a credible published but contested claim, not an established first arrival.

records.title: White Sands — repeated human trackmaking
records.siteName: White Sands National Park, New Mexico, United States
records.coordinatePrecision: Park visitor-center proxy; NOT the footprint locality; generalized geographic locator only

time.method: Conifer-pollen and aquatic-seed radiocarbon dating; OxCal 4.4.4 / IntCal20; earlier independent quartz OSL checks
time.conversion: 1950 minus 23500 and 21700; aggregate footprint sequence, not continuous residence

records.claim: Multiple footprint horizons document repeated human presence during the Last Glacial Maximum.
records.explanation: The October 2026 study refines the expanded footprint sequence to 23.5–21.7 ka. An outlined interval represents the aggregate dating envelope; it is not evidence that a settlement remained occupied in every intervening year.
records.discussion: Earlier dates based on aquatic seeds raised objections about old carbon and redeposition. Pigati and colleagues tested that chronology with terrestrial pollen and quartz luminescence in 2023. The newer chronology adds pollen analyses. Cultural affiliation and migration direction remain unassigned; footprints cannot establish either on their own.

support.claim: Independent chronological checks and historical objections

records.title: Monte Verde II — late Pleistocene dating interpretation
records.coordinatePrecision: Generalized complex locator, rounded to 0.01 degrees

time.method: Radiocarbon and stratigraphic interpretation; contextual OSL
time.conversion: 1950 - 14500 = -12550; rounded reference year only, not an exact annual date or duration

records.claim: One interpretation dates the MV-II cultural component to approximately 14,500 cal BP.
records.explanation: The earlier interpretation associates structures, hearths, and artifacts with a late-Pleistocene surface. The displayed year represents this published interpretation, not the resolution of the dating evidence.
records.discussion: Surovell and colleagues proposed a Middle Holocene age in 2026, invoking alluvial chronology and a tephra relationship. Waters and colleagues dispute the terrace correlations and evidence for redeposition. These competing interpretations must remain distinct; do not average them into one date or imply occupation throughout the interval separating them.

support.locator: Previous work at Monte Verde; chronology

records.displayCaution: An approximate single-year reference is not an exact occurrence. Show a tilde/approximate label and provide jump-to-record navigation; do not silently manufacture an uncertainty window.

records.title: Chinchihuapi CH-I — later projectile-point and hearth context
records.siteName: Chinchihuapi CH-I, Monte Verde complex, Chile
records.coordinatePrecision: Generalized complex locator; CH-I is a separate locality, not the MV-II excavation

time.conversion: 1950 minus calibrated endpoints; uncertain occurrence range, not a 31-year residence

records.claim: Dillehay and colleagues report a later CH-I context containing a projectile point, hearth, and drill fragment.
records.explanation: This younger context is separate from the MV-II interpretation. Similarity to Paiján forms does not establish the makers' identity or a migration link.
records.discussion: This is a bounded record of the published context, not independent replication of the excavation. Do not fill the intervening millennia with occupation or transfer the MV-II dispute automatically to every nearby context.

records.title: L’Anse aux Meadows — Norse woodworking in 1021 CE
records.coordinatePrecision: Generalized property locator rounded from UNESCO coordinates; not individual sample findspots

time.method: Annual tree rings matched to the 993 CE radiocarbon anomaly

records.claim: Wood modified with metal tools in Norse archaeological contexts dates to cutting activity in 1021 CE.
records.explanation: Kuitems and colleagues identified the 993 CE radiocarbon signal in three different trees and counted annual rings to their outer edges. Agreement among the resulting cutting dates anchors Norse activity to 1021.
records.discussion: This precise date does not date the settlement's founding or abandonment. It also does not show that every Norse activity occurred in that year. No arrival route is inferred from this record.

support.claim: 1021 CE activity and Norse archaeological association
support.locator: Precise dating of Norse activity in the Americas; Fig. 2

records.title: Cahokia — urban archaeological complex

time.method: Archaeological chronology synthesized with regional environmental evidence
time.conversion: CE years retained; endpoints are approximate scholarly period boundaries

records.claim: Cahokia's urban complex belongs to a Mississippian occupation phase approximately 1050–1400 CE.
records.explanation: This row represents the urban phase, not the first or last human presence in the region. Mississippian is an archaeological classification, not a race.
records.discussion: The regional population persisted and later increased. Ending this marker must not imply an empty watershed or extinction.

support.claim: Urban phase and regional continuity distinction

records.title: Monks Mound — River L’Abbe mission
records.siteName: Monks Mound, Cahokia archaeological complex, Illinois
records.coordinatePrecision: Generalized complex locator; not a surveyed church footprint

time.method: Historical chronology reported in a peer-reviewed archaeological synthesis

records.claim: The River L’Abbe mission operated at Monks Mound between 1735 and 1752 CE.
records.explanation: White and colleagues describe Cahokia people relocating to the Horseshoe Lake area and a French mission established on Monks Mound. This is a later historical episode, not continuation of the medieval urban polity.
records.discussion: The dates delimit the mission's operation. The later destination of every resident is not established here. Original cited historical studies were not independently reviewed.

records.title: Louisiana Purchase Treaty
records.siteName: Louisiana territory; treaty concluded in Paris
records.coordinatePrecision: No point marker: a territorial diplomatic event is not a settlement location

time.method: Dated treaty in an authenticated archival collection
time.conversion: Year-level timeline uses 1803 CE; full date preserved

records.claim: The United States and France concluded the Louisiana Purchase Treaty in 1803.
records.explanation: The National Archives preserves the treaty and identifies its provenance in Record Group 11. This primary document supports a dated diplomatic transaction and the application's chronological endpoint.
records.discussion: The treaty expresses the claims of its signatory governments. It is not evidence that the territory was unoccupied, that Indigenous peoples consented, or that populations moved in the year of signature. Keep it in the event table and timeline without a fabricated settlement dot.

support.locator: Archival citation, preamble, Articles I and VI, closing date
